First, I want to thank Council and the GRT staff for bringing forward this pilot.
Offering one free transit day per week for those aged 65 and older is an important step toward making our region and community more age-friendly.
Mobility is not just about transportation.
It's about independence and social connection and access to essential services.
In Waterloo Region, older adults now account for roughly 40% of emergency shelter occupancy.
Access to reliable transportation can be the difference between maintaining stability and becoming disconnected from housing, health care, and community supports.
I want to acknowledge the work staff have done in developing an implementation plan that allows for evaluation and data collection.
Council needs evidence to determine whether this is an important and useful program, and that it is entirely reasonable to collect this data.
However, I want to raise a concern about relying solely on the GRT payout as the gateway for participation.
The staff reports note that digital adoption among older adults is widespread, with over 85% of seniors in Ontario using the internet and high smartphone ownership.
However, using the internet and using a specific smartphone app are not the same thing.
Many older adults who are comfortable checking email, reading the news, using Facebook,
still face barriers when asked to download and manage a mobile app that includes registration and payments.
Many older adults will face barriers related to digital literacy, disability, accessibility, or comfort with technology.
Many who own smartphones rely on families, staff, or community centres and librarians
to help them navigate apps and digital services.
It is also important to recognise the financial realities many older adults face.
Roughly 35% in this region live in poverty, meaning that they may not have reliable data plans,
newer smartphones, or the digital supports needed to participate easily in an app-based program.
If the goal of the pilot is to understand how free transit affects older adults,
the pilot itself should not unintentionally exclude some of the people it is meant to serve.
I understand that the app is attractive because it provides clean, useful data,
But evaluation does not depend on an app.
Transit systems already collect extensive data through automatic passenger counts, operator tellers, and before and after ridership comparisons, methods used widely when evaluating fare changes.
For example, other communities like Barrie and Halifax rely on simple ID verification and aggregate ridership data
rather than requiring a specific tech platform.
Another concern that sometimes arises is misuse.
But other transit systems address this through a reasonable ID verification programs
or operator discretion.
Approaches that are simple, low cost, and widely used across Canada.
This is why I believe a hybrid approach deserves consideration.
The app can remain an option for those who prefer it and for collecting useful data.
But there should also be a low barrier alternative for older adults who cannot or do not wish to use an app.
This must be stressed.
